conclusion.label: rejects

report:
## Conclusion

No — current best evidence does not support coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) as an effective treatment for improving movement symptoms in Parkinson's disease.

An earlier Phase II trial suggested that CoQ10 (300–1200 mg/day) might slow progressive decline in early, untreated PD as measured by the UPDRS, generating initial optimism (https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/clinical-trials/effects-coenzyme-q10-coq-parkinson-disease; https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/782965). However, this finding needed confirmation in a larger trial.

That confirmation came in the form of a large, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind Phase III trial (Beal et al.) testing high-dosage CoQ10 in early Parkinson's disease. This definitive study found no clinical benefit — CoQ10 did not slow disease progression or improve motor symptoms compared to placebo, and the trial was stopped for futility (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/1851409; https://www.alzforum.org/news/research-news/coenzyme-q10-strikes-out-phase-3-parkinsons).

A subsequent systematic review of CoQ10 in Parkinsonian syndromes similarly notes that while CoQ10 has theoretical antioxidant/mitochondrial support relevant to PD's pathophysiology, and lower tissue CoQ10 levels have been observed in PD patients, this has not translated into demonstrated clinical efficacy for motor symptoms (https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4426/12/6/975).

**Bottom line:** Despite a plausible biological rationale (oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in PD) and encouraging early Phase II signals, the more rigorous, larger Phase III trial definitively showed CoQ10 does not improve movement symptoms or slow disease progression in Parkinson's disease. It is not recommended as a treatment for PD motor symptoms based on current evidence.
